paragraphs: In the morning, validate layouts and shading using irradiance data. At midday, coordinate the interconnection plan with electrical engineers. In the afternoon, run generation simulations to assess efficiency. In the evening, issue design releases. At month's end, sign off on grid connection and generation results.

In short: turn sunlight into electricity delivered to the grid. Duties include defining layouts, simulating and comparing options, coordinating electrical interconnection, controlling efficiency and cost, following construction and grid connection, and driving operations and maintenance. Combining analytical work with field activity, these engineers serve as the hub of photovoltaic projects.

Data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) show that about 158,800 solar energy systems engineers were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to rise to 162,100 by 2034, a net increase of about 3,300 jobs, with approximately 9,300 openings each year. The median annual wage was about $117,800 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace this occupation, but it will accelerate design. Generation forecasting and layout optimization speed up routine calculations, shifting engineers from calculating irradiance toward defining systems, managing interconnection, and taking responsibility on site. People who only perform basic calculations will be displaced, while those who understand both integration and the grid will become more valuable.
